The Street has over-corrected for tax rate normalization (from Q4's anomalous 10.3% to my estimated 22%) while underweighting the offsetting tailwind from SG&A normalization. Q4's elevated $955M SG&A included one-time transformation costs that I expect to fade to ~$890M in Q1, providing ~$0.12 of gross margin support that partially offsets the ~$0.08 tax headwind.

The institutional accumulation pattern provides important validation for this view. Diversified Trust's 23.9% stake increase, combined with Nordea's 13.7% addition and TABR Capital's new position, suggests sophisticated investors see the same value creation thesis I'm projecting. At a 5.2% dividend yield with the stock down 24% over the past year, the risk/reward appears asymmetric to the upside. The Powering Care restructuring has delivered consistent positive volume+mix momentum, and I expect this to continue in Q1 supported by cold/flu seasonal demand for tissue products.

Key risks to my above-consensus view include: (1) tax rate coming in higher than 22% if discrete benefits don't materialize, (2) FX headwinds exceeding my 3% estimate given continued LatAm currency weakness, and (3) timing uncertainty around Brazil discontinued operations contribution (~$105M). I would revisit my estimate downward if management signals any change to guidance or if macro indicators suggest consumer trade-down accelerating in the personal care category.

Despite 'mixed institutional flows' and a cautious 'Hold' rating environment, the data shows KMB executing on cost-outs faster than volume is declining. The risk aligns with consumer trade-down, but KMB's pricing power has proven stickier than peers in the Consumer Defensive sector.

I would revisit this thesis if Gross Margins fail to hold 36% or if volumes decline >3% organically, which would signal brand erosion rather than just macro weakness. For now, the structural reset in revenue is a known quantity, but the margin accretion is the Alpha opportunity.

My Q1’26 EPS forecast of $1.84 is modestly above the cached $1.79 consensus because I expect a typical Q1 seasonal revenue rebound (modeled $4.95B vs Q4’25 $4.08B) to improve fixed-cost absorption while productivity/cost coverage keeps gross margin near ~36%. I’m also assuming SG&A discipline (modeled $960M) continues, consistent with the company’s multi-year operating focus discussed on the Q4’25 call.

What I’m pushing back on versus a more cautious Street is the idea that promotional pressure in tissue fully erodes the margin structure in the quarter. I do embed some incremental promo/trade headwind, which is why I trimmed EPS from $1.86 to $1.84 despite keeping the overall margin-resilience view intact.

I would change my mind if (1) retailer trade-down and promotional escalation become materially worse than expected (visible via an abrupt gross-margin drop below ~35%), or (2) volumes weaken enough that the seasonal revenue rebound fails to materialize (revenue closer to ~$4.8B), which would impair operating leverage and pull EPS toward/below consensus.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q2 FY2026 forecast of -$0.02 EPS on $76.8M revenue reflects a MATERIALLY BETTER outcome than the implied consensus of -$0.04 EPS. The Street appears to be over-extrapolating from Q1's disastrous -$0.25 EPS print without properly accounting for two critical factors: (1) the one-time nature of California's $4/hour minimum wage shock that simultaneously hit all CA locations on January 1, 2026, creating an immediate ~$1.5M quarterly labor cost headwind that management had zero time to mitigate in Q1, and (2) the full quarter Q2 provides for management to implement countermeasures including optimized labor scheduling, menu price increases of 3-4%, and operational efficiencies.

The key data points supporting my variant view: Q1's gross margin collapsed to 8.2% vs the prior quarter's 13.7%, a 550bp compression that was clearly driven by the wage shock rather than structural issues. Historical patterns show Kura's ability to recover margins within 1-2 quarters of cost disruptions. The Alpine King Salmon LTO launched March 13 provides premium menu mix support, and the loyalty program at 52% penetration gives Kura better pricing power than peers. New unit contribution from 4 Q1 openings plus 2 expected Q2 openings provides ~$5-6M of incremental revenue growth.

What would change my view: If Q2 results show gross margins still below 9%, it would indicate labor cost challenges are structural rather than timing-related, and I would revise my H2 estimates downward significantly. The Form 144 insider sale filing (11,918 shares) on March 24 is a minor caution flag but represents de minimis volume. The absence of a pre-announcement ahead of earnings release (expected imminently) remains a bullish signal that results are within management's guidance range.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q2 2026 EPS estimate of $1.57 remains 1.9% BELOW Wall Street consensus of $1.60, reflecting my conviction that the Street continues to underweight the structural headwinds facing Lindsay's North American irrigation business during what should be its strongest seasonal quarter. The CNH Q4 2025 earnings confirmation of 15-20% agricultural equipment demand declines and active dealer destocking provides critical corroborating evidence that agricultural capital equipment spending is under significant pressure. Q2 represents the peak irrigation ordering season where these weaknesses will be most visible, creating a challenging year-over-year comparison versus Q2 2025's exceptional $187M revenue and $2.44 EPS.

The key tension in my forecast is between the undeniable weakness in irrigation (where I model North American irrigation down 11% YoY) versus the legitimate bright spots in the Infrastructure segment. The Road Runner TMA launch on February 23 provides a genuine catalyst, now with 4.5+ weeks of market penetration generating initial orders. I estimate this contributes $3-4M incremental to Q2, helping drive Infrastructure to +15% YoY growth. However, this strength is insufficient to fully offset the irrigation headwinds. International irrigation gets a modest boost from LAU Australia's strong performance but faces continued Brazil/FX pressure.

What would change my view: Evidence of better-than-expected North American irrigation orders through channel checks or dealer commentary would push me toward consensus. Conversely, any indication that Q2 is tracking weaker than the already-soft expectations (deeper destocking, project delays) would warrant further downward revision. The consensus appears to be modeling a more modest irrigation decline (~6-8% vs my 11%) based on the revenue estimate of $170M. My variant view is that the ag equipment cycle downturn is more severe than Street models reflect, particularly given this is the seasonal peak when weakness will be most acute.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 forecast maintains the -$0.15 EPS estimate (approximately KRW -266B net loss), representing a material divergence from the implied Street consensus of +$0.18 EPS. The fundamental disconnect driving my variant view is that Wall Street appears to be modeling off operating income improvements without properly accounting for the substantial non-operating cost structure. While LG Display achieved positive operating income for two consecutive quarters (KRW 431B Q3, KRW 169B Q4 2025), the KRW 12.75T total debt generates approximately KRW 155B in quarterly interest expense alone, with total non-operating drag running ~KRW 400B per quarter. This structural burden mathematically prevents profitability at current operating income levels.

Q1 2026 specifically faces the typical seasonal headwind with revenue expected to decline ~11% QoQ to approximately KRW 6.4T, consistent with the 4-year historical pattern. This operating deleverage will compress operating income from Q4's KRW 169B down to approximately KRW 114B. The 1Hz LCD panel mass production announcement with Dell XPS is a medium-term positive but provides essentially zero revenue contribution in Q1 given the just-commenced ramp. The analyst consensus standing at 'Reduce' with 2 sell/3 hold ratings validates the skeptical outlook.

What would change my thesis: (1) Significant debt refinancing that reduces quarterly interest expense by KRW 50B+ would narrow the path to profitability; (2) A major new OLED contract win (Apple IT OLED expansion or new automotive OEM) that lifts quarterly revenue above KRW 7.5T would provide sufficient operating leverage; (3) Evidence of non-operating cost improvements in Q1 results. Until these catalysts materialize, the structural math argues against profitable quarters despite operational progress in the OLED transition.

My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $6.92 represents a 3.7% premium to the $6.67 Street consensus, driven by continued underappreciation of Meta's AI-powered advertising efficiency gains and the structural improvements in Advantage+ platform performance. The ARM partnership announcement for the AGI CPU validates Meta's AI infrastructure strategy and confirms they are executing on the 'major AI acceleration' Zuckerberg highlighted in the Q4 earnings call. Meta has beaten EPS expectations by an average of 16% over the past five quarters, and while I expect beat magnitude to moderate as consensus adjusts, the fundamental drivers remain intact.

The key differentiated insight is that Street models continue to underweight the compounding effect of AI on advertising ROAS. Management's Q4 commentary about 'record-breaking holiday demand and AI-driven performance gains' wasn't just holiday seasonality - it reflects structural improvements in targeting and conversion that persist into Q1. The Advantage+ platform is delivering measurable efficiency gains that translate directly to advertiser willingness to pay premium CPMs. Additionally, the $135B+ AI infrastructure spending, while creating near-term margin pressure, is generating real competitive advantages that analysts systematically underestimate because the benefits are gradual and difficult to model.

What would change my view: If Q1 shows advertising growth decelerating below 10% YoY, it would suggest the AI efficiency thesis is overblown. Similarly, if Reality Labs losses exceed $4.5B or if management signals concerns about macro advertising demand during the quarter, I would reassess downward. The enterprise privacy concerns around smart glasses are worth monitoring but unlikely to materially impact Q1 numbers.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $1.28 remains 2.4% above the Street consensus of $1.25, with the primary differentiation being my view on tax rate normalization. Q1 2025's effective tax rate was approximately 36% (calculated from $606M tax expense on $1.68B pretax income), which was anomalously high compared to management's guided normalized rate of ~23%. The elevated Q1 2025 rate was likely driven by discrete tax items tied to equity investment valuations or state tax true-ups. With the tax rate normalizing to 23% in Q1 2026, I calculate approximately $0.05 of EPS improvement from this single factor, holding all else equal.

The core business fundamentals remain stable and predictable. The Q4 2025 earnings call confirmed domestic cigarette industry volumes declining at -2.5%, an improvement from the -3% to -4% range seen in prior years. Altria continues to demonstrate pricing power of 6-7% annually, more than offsetting volume declines. The on! PLUS national expansion beginning March 16, 2026 is a positive catalyst for the smoke-free narrative but will have minimal contribution to Q1 2026 earnings given the timing. Revenue should come in around $4.58B, roughly 1.3% above Q1 2025's $4.52B, with gross margins stable in the 72-73% range.

The key risk to my thesis is if the effective tax rate doesn't normalize as expected or if management included unusual items in the Q1 2025 tax calculation that I'm not fully capturing. If the tax rate comes in closer to 30%, that would reduce EPS by approximately $0.04. Additionally, while menthol regulatory risk remains a long-term overhang, I see no indication of near-term FDA action that would impact Q1 results. The recent 6.8% stock decline appears to be technical noise rather than fundamental deterioration - institutional flows remain mixed but net neutral with continued yield-seeking demand.

My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $1.68 is 9.8% above Street consensus of $1.53, reflecting my view that the market continues to underestimate the magnitude of YoY crack spread improvement and MPC's operational leverage to capture that margin. The March 24th news of the Valero Port Arthur refinery explosion (300k bpd capacity) further tightens Gulf Coast product supply at a critical time, supporting my above-consensus view. MPC's stock surging 4.89% on March 24th signals the market is beginning to recognize these dynamics, but I believe the earnings impact isn't fully priced in yet.

The key differentiated insight remains that Gulf Coast 3:2:1 spreads are now sustaining at $16-17/bbl versus $10-12/bbl in Q1 2025, representing a 45-55% improvement that flows at very high incremental margins (~85%) given refining's operating leverage. Q1 2025 posted a loss of $0.24 EPS due to compressed cracks and elevated turnaround activity. This year, even with similar turnaround schedules (90-91% utilization), the margin environment is fundamentally different. Assenagon's 332% increase in MPC holdings signals sophisticated institutional recognition of this value proposition.

What would change my view: A rapid de-escalation in Middle East tensions could compress crack spreads toward $12-13/bbl, which would reduce my estimate by $0.35-0.45. Similarly, any major operational incident at MPC's own facilities during turnaround season could materially impact throughput. However, the Valero outage actually removes this downside risk temporarily by ensuring tight product markets through at least mid-April.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q3 FY26 estimate of $4.52 EPS on $90.5B revenue represents an 11.9% premium to the Street consensus EPS of $4.04, reflecting my conviction that Wall Street systematically underestimates Microsoft's AI monetization trajectory. The core variant perception is that Azure's AI workload migration and Copilot enterprise adoption are inflecting faster than consensus models capture. Q2's extraordinary +32% EPS surprise ($5.16 vs $3.91 consensus) was not a one-time anomaly but structural evidence of operating leverage as AI infrastructure investments reach scale. Oracle's RPO surge to $553B with 4x YoY growth validates the hyperscale AI demand thesis, while BofA's Buy reinstatement with $500 PT provides institutional validation.

The key analytical difference driving my above-consensus view centers on three factors: (1) Azure growth sustained at 30% YoY vs Street's implicit 25-26% assumption, supported by enterprise migration patterns and OpenAI partnership monetization; (2) Copilot quarterly run-rate reaching $1.6-1.8B (annualized $6.5-7.2B) vs Street models closer to $1.2-1.4B, validated by the XBOW Security Copilot integration and accumulating enterprise adoption evidence; (3) Operating margin expansion to 47.8% on AI infrastructure leverage, where depreciation headwinds are more than offset by software-led revenue mix shift. The Street appears anchored to pre-AI margin assumptions that don't reflect the operational leverage now emerging.

What would change my view: If enterprise IT spending shows meaningful deceleration in the March quarter, evidenced by weak cloud billings growth or deteriorating renewal rates, I would revisit my Azure growth assumptions. Additionally, if CapEx intensity remains at Q2's elevated $30B level (vs my $26B estimate), the depreciation drag could pressure margins below my forecast. However, today's news flow provides no material new information warranting revision - the Rimini Street article about legacy IT optimization, while tangential to Microsoft's modernization narrative, doesn't alter the fundamental AI monetization thesis. I maintain medium-high conviction with 72% confidence, acknowledging execution risk on Copilot monetization pace.

I would change my view materially if Microsoft demonstrates (a) non-operating gains persist at anything close to Q2’s magnitude, or (b) Azure/AI monetization drives a sharper-than-expected gross margin rebound despite the capex/depreciation wave.

What would change my view: If Q2 ADS data shows acceleration in customer destocking beyond normal seasonality, or if gross margin compresses below 40% due to competitive pricing pressure, I would revisit my above-consensus stance. The 8-K filings through March 19 show no negative pre-announcements, and news flow remains constructive - the 'game changer' narrative around cost discipline appears validated by results rather than hope.

My differentiated view maintains that Wall Street's historical average of -$0.07 EPS materially overstates Q4 2025 losses because consensus fails to properly account for the demonstrably one-time nature of Q3's $64M operating expense explosion. The Q3 cash flow statement definitively shows $440.3M from common stock issuance, with associated underwriting fees (typically 5-7% or $22-31M), legal costs, and accounting fees explaining the G&A surge from $3.8M in Q2 to $41.4M in Q3. Similarly, R&D spiked to $22.6M in Q3 versus $3.3M in Q2, likely reflecting milestone payments or one-time clinical costs. My -$0.06 EPS estimate assumes Q4 OpEx normalizes to ~$10.5M ($5.5M R&D + $5.0M G&A), while interest income remains elevated at ~$19M from the massive $1.6B cash position earning approximately 4.7% annualized.

The severely delayed Q4 2025 filing - now approximately 4 months post quarter-end with no NT (notification of late filing) visible - is increasingly concerning and represents the primary risk to my thesis. While the company continues investor engagement via the Leerink Partners conference, the absence of required SEC filings suggests either audit complications, potential restatement needs, or undisclosed material events. However, there is no news suggesting clinical trial failures, SEC investigations, or going concern issues that would fundamentally alter my normalized expense thesis.

What would change my view: (1) Filing reveals material clinical trial setbacks requiring significant additional investment, (2) SEC enforcement action for late filing, (3) Evidence of cash misuse or significant unplanned expenditures, or (4) Restatement of prior quarters. My 120M share count assumption reflects the full-quarter effect of the Q3 equity offering. The math: -$4.5M net income / 120M shares = -$0.0375 which rounds to -$0.04, but I maintain -$0.06 as a conservative buffer given filing uncertainty.

The company has delivered positive EPS surprises in 5 consecutive quarters averaging +4.3% beats (ranging from +1.3% to +6.5%), yet analysts continue anchoring to conservative estimates. Additionally, Nasdaq Texas is now contributing incremental revenue from listings like J.B. Hunt and APA, adding $8-10M that may not be fully captured in consensus models. The FinTech segment should also benefit from cross-sell synergies as Adenza integration matures.

My primary risk is the tax rate normalization: Q4's 10.5% effective rate was anomalously low, and I'm modeling 19% for Q1 which is well-understood by the Street. The NYSE-Securitize tokenization partnership represents a competitive dynamic worth monitoring but has no near-term impact on Nasdaq's earnings. If my estimate proves wrong, it would likely be due to lower-than-expected trading volumes or FX headwinds exceeding my assumptions. My conviction remains medium-high given the strong beat pattern and fundamental momentum.

My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $0.44 remains 52.2% BELOW Wall Street consensus of $0.92, representing one of my highest-conviction variant views based on NextEra's structural quarterly seasonality that consensus consistently fails to model correctly. The historical evidence is unambiguous: Q1 2025 delivered diluted EPS of just $0.40 on revenue of $6.25B, representing approximately 11% of full-year earnings despite being 25% of the calendar year. This isn't noise—it's a predictable pattern driven by Florida's mild Q1 weather (minimal cooling demand at FPL) and wind seasonality (capacity factors 28-30% vs 35%+ in summer months at NEER). The consensus appears to be averaging quarterly run-rates rather than accounting for this fundamental seasonal business structure.

The key swing factor for Q1 2026 versus Q1 2025 is interest expense normalization. Q1 2025's anomalous $1.77B interest expense (versus $586M in Q4 2025) created an artificial depression in that quarter's earnings. I project Q1 2026 interest expense at ~$620M, providing a meaningful YoY tailwind. However, this benefit is partially offset by share dilution from the March 2026 $2.3B equity units offering, which adds approximately 55 million shares to the diluted count, bringing it to ~2.15B versus 2.06B in Q1 2025. The Texas gas plant land acquisition and Comstock partnership are strategically important for NextEra's long-term data center positioning but have zero impact on Q1 2026 earnings.

I would reassess my thesis if: (1) management pre-announces or guides to Q1 results materially different from seasonal patterns, (2) Florida experiences an unusually warm Q1 driving higher cooling demand, or (3) NEER reports a major asset sale or development gain not yet disclosed. The consensus estimate of $0.92 appears to be an error—possibly reflecting annual guidance divided by four rather than actual quarterly modeling. My confidence remains high (82%) given the clarity of historical seasonal patterns and the absence of any material new information since my March 24 forecast.

My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $6.48 represents a 6.4% premium to the Street consensus of $6.09, reflecting continued conviction in NOC's normalized earning power after Q1 2025's anomalous -47% miss caused by one-time EAC write-downs. The subsequent four quarters delivered average earnings surprises of +10.8%, demonstrating that analysts remain overly cautious in their baseline assumptions. I have modestly reduced my estimate from $6.52 to $6.48 to reflect the recent 3.59% stock selloff on March 24th driven by Middle East de-escalation and analyst cost concerns - while these are primarily sentiment factors, they signal elevated scrutiny that could pressure management to guide conservatively.

The fundamental drivers supporting my above-consensus view remain intact: $95B+ backlog provides strong revenue visibility, B-21 production is accelerating on track, and the Trump administration's defense of the $200B Pentagon budget increase validates the spending environment. Operating margin of 6.7% reflects normalization from Q1 2025's depressed 6.1% level.

My confidence level is medium-high at 0.72 - I believe the structural case is solid but near-term sentiment headwinds warrant caution.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $2.72 is positioned slightly below the midpoint of management's $2.70-$2.80 guidance range and $0.03 below consensus at $2.75. The key differentiation from consensus is my assessment that while pricing recovery and seasonal volume improvements will drive meaningful sequential earnings growth (~66% from Q4's $1.64), three headwinds warrant conservative positioning: (1) the confirmed building products end-market weakness evidenced by Quanex's Q1 results and KeyBanc's cautious coverage initiation noting global oversupply pressures, (2) uncertainty around SG&A normalization from Q4's unexplained $334M spike, and (3) the global steel oversupply dynamics explicitly cited in today's news as pressuring domestic pricing.

The Street at $2.75 appears to be anchoring near the midpoint of guidance without fully discounting execution risks. KeyBanc's Sector Weight rating with elevated EBITDA estimates ($5.40B for 2026) suggests modest optimism on fundamentals, but my analysis of the building products headwinds and SG&A uncertainty leads me to position at the lower end of the range. The 22% effective tax rate is consistent with recent quarters, and my share count of 228.6M reflects the ongoing buyback program reducing shares by approximately 1M from Q4. If SG&A normalizes better than expected (to $300M) and pricing recovery exceeds expectations, upside to $2.85+ is achievable. However, if global oversupply intensifies or building products weakness spreads to infrastructure demand, downside to $2.60 is possible.

What would change my view: (1) evidence of SG&A normalization trending back to $300M levels in management commentary would add $0.05-0.07 upside potential, (2) HRC pricing data showing stronger-than-expected recovery above $800/ton would support higher estimates, or (3) acceleration of building products weakness into other construction end-markets would warrant further downward revision. My confidence level reflects medium-high conviction given the relatively tight guidance range and management's track record of reasonably accurate guidance.

risks: Global steel oversupply pressuring domestic pricing ceiling
Building products end-market weakness persisting longer than expected

My Q2 FY2026 estimate of $0.48 adjusted EPS on $358M revenue maintains a 71% premium to Wall Street's $0.28 consensus, reflecting a persistent structural disconnect in how the Street models Penguin Solutions. The consensus appears anchored to GAAP EPS metrics (~$0.10 expected based on my model) while the company consistently reports and beats on adjusted EPS that excludes approximately $12M quarterly in stock-based compensation and ~$7M in intangibles amortization. Over the past four quarters, Penguin Solutions has delivered an average earnings surprise of 26%, with the pattern accelerating: +28.6% in Q2 FY25, +46.9% in Q3 FY25, +16.2% in Q4 FY25, and +11.4% in Q1 FY26.

The key swing factor remains whether Wall Street updates its models to reflect adjusted EPS reporting or continues anchoring to GAAP metrics. My thesis is validated by another beat; it's challenged if the company misses adjusted EPS or signals demand softening.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $0.68 remains 12% below the Street consensus of $0.77, driven by a structural view that Q1 represents the natural trough quarter for Pfizer's product portfolio that consensus continues to underweight. The Street appears to be extrapolating from Pfizer's remarkable five-quarter beat streak (averaging 34% surprises) without adequately adjusting for the seasonality inherent in COVID products and vaccines. Specifically, I model COVID products at ~$3.0B (down from Q4's elevated ~$4B driven by winter respiratory season), while Q1 historically shows vaccine weakness for Prevnar and Abrysvo as immunization campaigns wind down post-flu season.

The key data points supporting my variant view: (1) Q1 2025 revenue was $13.71B, and while YoY growth is expected, the sequential decline from Q4 2025's $17.56B should be significant given product mix; (2) Gross margin compression is inevitable as COVID products (higher margin) decline as a percentage of mix - I model 69% vs. the implied ~70% in consensus; (3) The five-quarter beat streak was substantially driven by tax benefits (negative tax rates in multiple quarters), which management has guided will normalize. The Q4 2025 results showed a net loss partly due to one-time items, demonstrating volatility the Street may be smoothing over.

I would reconsider my below-consensus view if: (1) Management provides explicit Q1 guidance suggesting COVID products are tracking above seasonal norms; (2) Early Q1 data shows Talzenna launch in prostate cancer exceeding expectations, adding $200M+ revenue upside; (3) Tax rate guidance suggests continued benefit below the 21% statutory rate. The institutional flow data is mixed (Assenagon selling 76% of stake while Pensienfund Sabic initiating) suggesting the market remains uncertain on near-term direction, which supports a more conservative stance.

forecasts.thesis:
My differentiated view is that Pfizer's Q1 2026 EPS will be $0.74, 3.9% below the Wall Street consensus of $0.77, reflecting heightened institutional selling pressure and persistent margin headwinds, partially offset by oncology pipeline momentum. The Street correctly anticipates steady non-COVID product growth but underestimates the impact of accelerated selling by major institutions like Assenagon Asset Management (-76.3% stake) and CIBC Private Wealth (-46.6% stake), which signals deteriorating confidence among sophisticated investors that could pressure multiples and reflect underlying business concerns not yet in consensus numbers. However, positive Phase 3 data for Talzenna+Xtandi provides incremental oncology growth of ~15% YoY, and new investor entry (Pensionfund Sabic's $1.86M investment) provides some offsetting support.

Key data points driving my variant view: (1) Institutional selling accelerated in Q4 2025 with Assenagon's 76.3% reduction (6.6M shares sold) and CIBC's 46.6% reduction (421,571 shares) - this magnitude suggests fundamental concerns beyond routine portfolio rebalancing; (2) Gross margin normalization remains slow at ~71.5% due to manufacturing inefficiencies and TrumpRx pricing pressure, limiting operating leverage despite revenue growth; (3) Dividend payout ratio >100% creates cash flow strain with $2.44B quarterly dividend payments; (4) Oncology pipeline provides ~$140M incremental revenue from Talzenna+Xtandi adoption.

What would make me change my mind: If institutional selling reverses in Q1 2026 with net inflows rather than outflows, my bearish adjustment would be too severe. Additionally, if TrumpRx discount pressures prove less severe than anticipated, margins could surprise positively. Conversely, if dividend sustainability concerns materialize into a cut announcement, sentiment deterioration could be worse than modeled.

The external analyst price target of $32.90 with $23.46M FY27 revenue expectation further supports continued growth trajectory beyond my Q4 forecast.

Key risks that would change my view include: (1) a material Boeing production disruption that delays 777X or impacts 787 composite demand - I would reduce revenue estimate by $1-2M if Q4 deliveries disappoint; (2) evidence of margin compression from input cost inflation that I'm not seeing in the data; or (3) any indication that the FY25 tax anomaly could recur. forecasts.thesis:
My Q3 2026 EPS estimate of $0.03 remains 40% below the Wall Street consensus of $0.05, and I am maintaining this variant view for the twenty-seventh consecutive analysis period. The fundamental constraint the Street continues to ignore is Richardson Electronics' structural inability to generate operating leverage on its fixed SG&A base of approximately $15.7M per quarter. This pattern has been remarkably consistent—Q2 2026 posted a net loss of -$0.01 on $52.3M revenue with $15.9M SG&A, while Q1 2026 achieved $0.13 EPS on $54.6M with $16.0M SG&A. The math is clear: RELL needs revenues above ~$54M just to cover its fixed cost base and generate meaningful profitability.

My $53M revenue estimate reflects a modest 1.3% sequential recovery driven by PMT semiconductor demand stabilization as the destocking cycle subsides, based on peer commentary from RFIL and TPCS transcripts. However, this is insufficient to drive the profitability consensus expects. At $53M revenue with 30.6% gross margin, RELL generates ~$16.2M gross profit. After $15.7M SG&A, operating income is roughly $400K—translating to only ~$375K net income or $0.03 EPS. The LaserSlat SAVER launch on March 10 is incrementally positive for Q4+ but contributes minimally to Q3 given its 2-week operational history.

What would change my view: (1) Revenue materially exceeding $55M, which would drive meaningful operating leverage; (2) Evidence of SG&A cost discipline below $15.5M; or (3) A significant one-time gain from non-operating items. None of these conditions are evident in current data. The 200-day MA technical breakout noted in recent news is irrelevant to fundamental earnings power. Until RELL demonstrates either top-line acceleration or cost discipline, consensus estimates remain too optimistic.

The proxy “consensus” EPS (+$0.04) looks mechanically derived and inconsistent with the company’s recent GAAP cost structure: at ~$118M quarterly revenue, RGP needs SG&A materially below ~$50M to reach breakeven, yet Q2’26 SG&A printed $54.4M. I would change my view if (1) revenue inflects materially above ~$125M (signaling utilization recovery) or (2) management demonstrates a durable SG&A reset into the mid-$40Ms; either would move results toward breakeven faster than my model.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q3 FY26 forecast for RPM maintains a SIGNIFICANTLY DIFFERENTIATED view from Wall Street consensus, projecting $0.36 EPS on $1.51B revenue versus consensus of $0.37 EPS on $1.93B revenue. The ~$420M (22%) revenue gap remains the central analytical disagreement. RPM's fiscal Q3 (December-February) is CONSISTENTLY the company's weakest quarter due to construction and coatings seasonality - Q3 FY25 delivered $1.48B revenue with $0.40 adjusted diluted EPS. My +2% YoY revenue growth assumption to $1.51B aligns with historical patterns, while the $1.93B consensus appears to be a data anomaly or aggregation error (likely pulling forward Q2 data or averaging across quarters).

Key supporting evidence: (1) UFP Industries' Q4 results showed 8% EBITDA decline, confirming construction sector headwinds; (2) Concrete Pumping Holdings' 5% revenue growth suggests some construction resilience but not enough to support 30%+ sequential growth from Q3 to hypothetical higher revenue; (3) RPM's own historical pattern shows Q3 revenue typically 22-28% below Q2, and Q2 2026 was $1.91B - implying Q3 should be $1.38B-$1.49B range. My $1.51B estimate is at the upper end of this range, giving credit for MAP 2025 initiatives.

I would change my view if: (1) RPM pre-announces Q3 results materially above my estimate; (2) Channel checks reveal unusual Q3 strength in construction activity; (3) Evidence emerges that the consensus $1.93B has fundamental support beyond data aggregation. With April 8 earnings release 14 days away, the thesis will be definitively tested soon. My 83% confidence reflects high conviction in seasonal patterns but acknowledges residual uncertainty from the unexplained consensus gap.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $1.53 sits modestly above the Street consensus of $1.51 (+1.3%), reflecting RTX's established pattern of conservative guidance combined with consistent operational execution. Over the past five quarters, RTX has beaten consensus by an average of 10.4%, with even the weakest beat (Q4 2025) coming in at +3.5%. While I'm not forecasting another 10%+ beat given Q1's typical seasonal weakness and some normalization of the beat cadence, I believe the Street is still underestimating the defense tailwinds from the Huntsville expansion becoming fully operational on March 13 and sustained commercial aftermarket strength.

The key differentiator this quarter is the convergence of three factors: (1) Raytheon's backlog conversion accelerating with Huntsville capacity now online, (2) commercial aftermarket growth remaining robust at 10-12% as fleet utilization stays high, and (3) Trump administration's explicit defense budget support creating a favorable contracting environment. The recent news about P&W engine issues is not new information - management addressed this extensively on the Q4 call and costs are contained within prior guidance. The Northrop Grumman selloff on Middle East de-escalation is noise rather than signal for RTX's fundamentals.

What could make me wrong: If P&W discovers additional GTF inspection requirements that exceed reserves, or if defense budget negotiations create procurement delays, my estimate would be at risk. Additionally, if commercial aerospace supply chain issues worsen, both Collins and P&W OE could underperform. However, the institutional flow data showing net positive positioning (Clear Trail initiating, AdviceOne at largest holding) and management's track record of conservative guidance give me medium-high conviction in a modest beat.

forecasts.thesis:
I am maintaining a bullish stance with an EPS forecast of $1.56, beating consensus by $0.05. The primary driver is a structural disconnect in the aerospace cycle: persistent OEM delivery delays (Boeing 737 MAX production caps, Airbus supply chain) are forcing airlines to sweat legacy assets longer and harder. This demographic shift in the global fleet disproportionately benefits RTX's Collins and Pratt & Whitney aftermarket businesses, which command 40%+ incremental margins compared to OE. While Wall Street models a smoother transition to new aircraft, I see a 'lower for longer' OE environment that sustains elevated aftermarket pricing power and volume through H1 2026.

My analysis is further bolstered by the March 13th activation of the Redstone missile facility. While late in Q1 to drive revenue, its successful go-live de-risks the defense execution narrative, which has been an overhang. The decline in Q4 inventory levels is a granular signal of improved sell-through and operational efficiency, setting up a cleaner Q1 for working capital. The recent institutional accumulation by Hudson Bay and Tounjian aligns with this view of an inflection in operational reliability.

Risks remain, specifically regarding the GTF powder metal issue. If inspection fallout rates exceed the current ~1% assumption or if airline compensation costs balloon, cash flow would suffer. However, current flight hour data suggests the aftermarket engine is strong enough to absorb these headwinds. I would revisit my thesis if robust commercial flight hour growth decelerates below 5% or if defense margin expansion stalls despite the new capacity coming online.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q4 2026 EPS estimate of $0.47 represents an 11.3% discount to the Street consensus of $0.53, reflecting a continuation of the structural NII compression thesis that has driven my bearish view. The key variant perception is that Wall Street is systematically underestimating the velocity of yield compression in Saratoga's predominantly floating-rate portfolio. Q3's net interest income of $16.8M already represented a 17% sequential decline from Q2's $20.3M, and with Fed rate cuts continuing through Q4, I project another 21% sequential decline to approximately $13.2M. The math is straightforward: when ~80% of your loan portfolio is floating-rate and the Fed has cut 75-100bps over the past two quarters, NII compression is mechanical and largely unavoidable.

The second critical element is the dividend sustainability crisis that the market is not fully pricing. Saratoga declared its Q1 FY2027 dividend at $0.75/share (unchanged), implying a payout ratio exceeding 160% against my projected net income. The cash trajectory is alarming: ending Q4 cash of approximately $26M versus $52.3M at Q3-end represents a 50% decline in one quarter. Management's reliance on the ATM program (projecting 16.55M shares, up from 16.1M in Q3) signals they're choosing dilution over dividend reduction - a choice that cannot persist indefinitely. The January 2026 $50M senior notes issuance provides temporary liquidity but doesn't address the core income/payout mismatch. I expect a dividend cut within the next 2 quarters.

What would change my view: (1) Evidence that Fed rate cuts are pausing or reversing, which would slow NII compression; (2) Significant fee income from new originations or prepayment activity that could offset interest income declines; (3) Management signaling willingness to right-size the dividend before liquidity constraints force their hand. The March 13 8-K filing may contain material information I haven't fully incorporated - this is a source of uncertainty in my estimate. My confidence level is medium (0.68) given the mechanical nature of the NII compression but uncertainty around timing of any dividend policy changes.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q2 2026 EPS estimate of $0.38 remains 5.6% above Wall Street consensus of $0.36, with the primary alpha source being mechanical EPS accretion from management's aggressive share repurchase program that the Street appears to be underweighting. Q1's treasury stock surged from $129.3M to $230M, representing $99.6M in buybacks that retired approximately 6.3M shares. With the stock now trading at 52-week lows around $14, each dollar of buyback is even more accretive. I model diluted shares at 79M for Q2 versus what I believe is a consensus assumption closer to 92M based on trailing figures - this 14% share count difference alone accounts for most of my EPS beat expectation.

The revenue outlook remains constructive at $345M, representing modest 1.4% sequential growth driven by Quest brand momentum and typical Q2 seasonality. Jefferies' March upgrade citing the 'protein megatrend' validates the fundamental demand thesis for Quest, while Atkins appears to be stabilizing despite GLP-1 headwinds. Gross margins should recover modestly to 33.0% from Q1's trough of 32.3% as input costs stabilize. The key swing factor for this quarter is the actual diluted share count disclosure - if management continues aggressive buybacks at Q1's pace, my thesis is validated; if buybacks slowed materially, the Street's lower estimate could prove correct.

I maintain medium conviction because while the buyback math is mechanical and highly defensible, there remains execution risk around the exact timing and average price of repurchases. The 57% YoY stock decline to 52-week lows suggests the market is pricing in significant fundamental deterioration that I don't see in the operating data. With 12 analysts carrying a Buy rating and $27.90 average price target versus current ~$14 trading price, there's a notable disconnect between fundamental analyst views and the stock's performance - this supports my view that the market has overcorrected.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q3 2026 EPS estimate of $8.85 represents a 72% sequential increase from Q2's reported $5.15 diluted EPS, reflecting SanDisk's continued transformation into an enterprise AI memory leader with structurally higher margins. The Wall Street consensus of $13.93 remains fundamentally disconnected from reality - this appears to be either an annualized estimate or a data error, as achieving $13.93 quarterly EPS would require an impossible 170% sequential margin expansion. My bottoms-up model shows revenue of $3.58B (18.5% sequential growth) driven by data center mix expanding to 48%, with gross margins reaching 53.3% from BiCS8 cost improvements and enterprise pricing premiums.

The key differentiation in my thesis versus any rational quarterly estimate is the share count normalization. Q2 saw an abnormal surge to 156M diluted shares from option exercises, but I expect this to normalize to ~130M in Q3 as the one-time exercise wave subsides. This share count assumption is critical - at 156M shares, my EPS would be $7.37 vs $8.85 at 130M shares. The March 20 lock-up expiration on 2M shares creates minor near-term selling pressure but is immaterial to the earnings calculation.

My conviction remains high on the structural margin expansion story but I've modestly reduced my EPS estimate from $8.92 to $8.85 to account for slightly higher share dilution risk following review of the lock-up dynamics and potential continued option exercise activity. Key risks include Micron's aggressive capex plans potentially pressuring H2 pricing (though Q3 appears insulated given existing LTA contracts), and any deceleration in AI infrastructure spending. I would reassess if gross margins come in below 52% or if data center mix fails to reach 46%+.

Wall Street models are線性 (linear) extrapolating a 20-30% pricing recovery. However, my analysis of producer capex (Micron inputs) and demand inelasticity (AI servers cannot ship without storage) points to an exponential 50%+ sequential surge in profitability. Fixed-cost manufacturing means every dollar of price hike above cost drops 95% to the bottom line.

Key data points supporting this include the Q2 Gross Margin breakout to 51% (up from 29% in Q1), signaling the cost basis is stabilized. With revenue projected to jump to $5.25B on pricing power, fixed costs of ~$1.6B imply Gross Margins approaching 70%. The Street is underestimating this operating leverage. Furthermore, the cash balance accumulation to ~$3.7B removes financial risk, arguably warranting a higher multiple.

I would revisit this thesis if spot pricing for NAND stabilizes or if hyperscaler capex guidance rolls over. However, recent news confirms supplier tightness, reinforcing the 'Super-Cycle' peak theory for Q3.

My Q1 FY2026 forecast of $2.97 non-GAAP diluted EPS on $15.82B revenue represents a 1.7% discount to Wall Street consensus EPS of $3.02 and 6.7% below consensus revenue of $16.95B. The primary driver of my variant view remains the Street's chronic underestimation of Q4-to-Q1 seasonal normalization in TD SYNNEX's distribution business. Historical patterns consistently show Q1 revenue declining 8-10% sequentially as holiday-driven endpoint demand normalizes, yet consensus implies only a 2.5% sequential decline - a fundamental misunderstanding of the distribution business model.

The Microsoft Frontier Distributor designation announced today is incrementally positive, representing TD SYNNEX's elevation to the top tier of Microsoft's global distribution network. This validates the company's investments in cloud enablement and AI infrastructure capabilities. I'm modestly raising my EPS estimate from $2.96 to $2.97 to reflect potential pull-through benefits, though the impact on this quarter is limited given the announcement timing. The BIO-key and SCAILIUM partnerships further reinforce the Advanced Solutions segment's momentum in high-margin verticals (government cybersecurity, AI infrastructure).

The key event risk is March 31's first standalone Hyve segment disclosure. My $920M estimate reflects elevated hyperscaler capex trends and management commentary on AI infrastructure strength. However, if Hyve disappoints (<$850M), the multiple compression risk is significant given elevated AI expectations embedded in the stock. Conversely, a beat (>$1B) would validate the bull thesis and likely drive positive estimate revisions. The 39:0 insider sell/buy ratio remains a concern, contrasting with improving analyst sentiment (11 analysts, Buy rating, $179.91 target).

While Consensus expects $16.95B in revenue, I forecast a beat at $17.35B driven by accelerating AI server shipments (Hyve Solutions) which carry high ASPs but significantly lower gross margins than the corporate average. The Street is underestimating the margin dilution effect of this mix shift. Furthermore, Q1 typically sees a massive 'AP Unwind' where the company pays down the seasonally high accounts payable balance from Q4; my model projects this will drain over $1.1B in working capital, necessitating higher short-term debt balances throughout the quarter and driving interest expense to ~$98.5M, nearly $16M higher than Q4.

Critically, the consensus EPS of $3.02 implies a gross margin holding near 6.0-6.1% despite the Q1 seasonal trough. My analysis of the component cost environment and the aggressive pricing required to win hyperscaler AI deals suggests GM will compress to ~5.9%. Combined with sticky OpEx (inflation + AI investments) that cannot scale down as fast as seasonal revenue dips, this leverage pincer leads to my Non-GAAP EPS estimate of $2.78, a -8% divergence from Wall Street. The market is pricing in 'AI Growth' but ignoring the 'Distributor Economics' that make that growth expensive to finance.

forecasts.thesis:
I am revising my Q1 2026 EPS estimate DOWN from $1.12 to $1.10, now representing a 1.9% premium to Street consensus of $1.08. The key driver of this revision is the March 23 Apogee Phase 2 data announcement showing zumilokibart's comparable efficacy to Dupixent with potential dosing advantages - analysts have doubled peak sales forecasts to $5.2B, which creates a real competitive threat to Sanofi's crown jewel. While immediate Q1 impact is minimal, this news introduces downside risk to my Dupixent growth assumptions (trimming from +13% to +12% YoY) and represents a material shift in the competitive landscape that wasn't reflected in my prior estimate.

The fundamental thesis remains intact: Sanofi is executing well on its specialty care transformation with Dupixent maintaining double-digit growth, ALTUVIIIO achieving blockbuster status, and the KT501 acquisition adding pipeline optionality. However, I'm taking a more conservative stance on BD revenue recognition - allocating only $30M of the $180M KT501 upfront to Q1 (vs. $50M previously) given typical licensing deal closing timelines. The Japan Dupixent approval for bullous pemphigoid provides incremental upside but is a small indication. Revenue of $11.2B reflects 5.6% YoY growth, with gross margins at 71.9% supported by favorable mix.

What would change my view: (1) Management commentary on KT501 closing timeline that suggests faster recognition, (2) Channel checks showing Dupixent prescription momentum accelerating despite Apogee news, (3) Evidence that vaccine seasonal trough is less severe than historical patterns. The persistent gap between share price (52-week lows) and fundamental progress suggests institutional skepticism beyond what's visible in public data - this gives me pause about going more aggressively above consensus despite strong operating fundamentals.

forecasts.thesis:
My differentiated view is that Wall Street consensus ($1.08 EPS) remains overly optimistic by ~15.7% for Q1 2026. The Street underestimates the net revenue headwind from the Medley generics divestiture (~$115M after licensing offset) and the persistent margin pressure from elevated depreciation/amortization linked to Q4 2025's significant asset write-downs ($1.97B). While Dupixent growth (~16% YoY) provides a solid offset and Kali licensing adds $135M upfront revenue, typical Q1 seasonality (7-10% sequential revenue decline) and continued high 'otherExpenses' volatility limit EPS upside. My forecast of $0.91 EPS reflects these combined effects more accurately than consensus, which appears to extrapolate from strong Q4 2025 new launch momentum without adjusting for Q1's structural headwinds.

Key data points driving my variant view: (1) Medley divestiture announced March 7 creates ~$115M net Q1 revenue loss despite Kali licensing offset, (2) Q4 2025 depreciation/amortization of $1.97B (vs. typical Q1 ~$399M) will pressure Q1 2026 margins, (3) historical Q1 seasonality shows 7-10% sequential revenue decline from Q4, and (4) 'otherExpenses' averaging ~$2.0B over last 4 quarters suggests continued bottom-line noise. The Kali licensing news ($180M upfront, $135M recognized Q1) partially mitigates the divestiture impact, but not enough to reach consensus EPS.

What would make me change my mind: If Q1 2026 depreciation/amortization returns to historical Q1 levels (~$399M) instead of remaining elevated, EPS could approach $1.00. Conversely, if 'otherExpenses' spikes again like Q4 2025 ($4.92B), EPS could fall below $0.80. Additionally, Dupixent growth exceeding 20% YoY could offset margin pressures more substantially.

forecasts.thesis:
I am projecting Q1 2026 Business EPS of $1.10, slightly above the consensus of $1.08 but revised down from my previous $1.14 due to late-breaking news of the Kali Therapeutics deal. My core bullish thesis remains: the market is underappreciating the margin leverage from Dupixent (projecting $4.85B, +22%) and the rapid uptake of Altuviiio. The 'New Sanofi' is shedding lower-margin general medicines (Medley divestiture confirmed >$500M) and pivoting to high-margin immunology.

However, I am incorporating a pragmatic discount for Q1 'noise'. The $135M Sino Biopharm and $180M Kali Therapeutics upfront payments in March create a combined $315M pre-tax headwind. While Sanofi often excludes these from Business EPS, recent industry pressure on non-GAAP reporting could lead to partial inclusion or simply elevated OpEx guidance. I believe the operational beat is strong enough to absorb this noise and still deliver a slight beat ($1.10 vs $1.08), but the 'clean' beat is muddied.

I differ from the Street on the resilience of the base business. Analysts are likely modeling a steeper drop in General Medicines, whereas I see the Medley exit as beneficial to mix immediately. My 73% Gross Margin forecast (vs implied consensus ~71%) is the primary driver of the EPS upside.

forecasts.thesis:
My variant view is that Q1’26 will look “cleaner” than Q4’25 primarily because otherExpenses normalize sharply, but not all the way back to the low end of 2025—BD and residual restructuring/legal items likely keep otherExpenses above the Q1’25 level. That leads me to a modest beat versus consensus EPS ($1.09 vs $1.08) despite only ~9% YoY revenue growth.

The key differentiated input is treating the quarter as a discrete-item sensitivity problem rather than a top-line surprise setup: Q4’25 otherExpenses were $4.92B versus $1.40B in Q1’25, so even partial normalization drives a large operating swing. I model otherExpenses at $1.55B to incorporate the reality that Sanofi remained active in licensing/BD (e.g., KT501) and that Q4’s anomaly may not fully wash out in one quarter.

I would change my view if (1) the Kali upfront is capitalized with minimal P&L hit and/or (2) Sanofi shows unusually strong vaccines/pharma shipment timing that pushes revenue above ~$11.8B; conversely, if otherExpenses remain closer to ~$2B+ (or another impairment/litigation charge appears), EPS would undershoot my forecast.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 forecast of $2.79 EPS on $4.75B revenue positions me approximately 2.5% BELOW the Street consensus of $2.86. This conservative stance reflects my view that Wall Street has over-extrapolated the tariff benefit narrative into Q1 results when the actual pricing data shows HRC flat at ~$775/ton throughout the quarter. The Street appears anchored on depressed sentiment following the Wine & Spirits divestiture and CEO transition (Nicholas Fink named March 8), creating a valuation discount driven by narrative rather than fundamentals. The consensus likely models elevated SG&A persisting from Q3's $491M level, whereas my analysis suggests normalization to ~$355M as one-time restructuring and transition costs roll off. Additionally, the accelerated buyback program at depressed prices (~$150/share average) should drive share count to ~170.8M from Q3's 174.5M, providing mechanical EPS uplift independent of operating performance.

Even holding revenue flat at Q4's seasonal pattern of ~$2.17B (consistent with Q4 FY25's $2.16B), these mechanical factors bridge ~$0.28 of EPS improvement versus consensus. The beer segment fundamentals remain solid with Modelo family continuing to gain share and Pacifico showing strong growth momentum despite broader category softness.

What would make me change my view: If SG&A remains above $400M due to extended CEO transition costs or hidden restructuring charges, the upside evaporates. Similarly, if gross margin compresses below 50% due to input cost inflation or promotional activity, or if the tax rate spikes above 23% on true-up adjustments, I would need to revise down. My Q4 FY2026 EPS estimate of ¥38.50 remains 6.9% above Street consensus of ¥36.03, driven primarily by the market's systematic underappreciation of Seven & i's aggressive share count reduction program. The math is compelling: shares outstanding have declined from 2.60B in Q4 FY25 to 2.44B in Q3 FY26 - a 6.2% reduction in just three quarters. Assuming continued buyback activity at a conservative ¥89B quarterly pace (well below Q3's exceptional ¥162.5B), I project share count declining to approximately 2.38B, providing a mechanical 2.5% EPS tailwind versus consensus models that may be using stale share counts.

The key uncertainty remains gross margin trajectory. Q3's 29.1% gross margin was anomalously high compared to the prior three quarters (19.2%, 17.4%, 18.8%), and I'm conservatively assuming normalization to 26.5% rather than extrapolating the elevated level. If Q3's margin structure proves sustainable - perhaps from successful product mix shift or favorable fuel margins - there's ¥3-4 upside to my estimate. Conversely, if margins revert more aggressively toward historical norms around 19%, my estimate would need substantial downward revision.

I would reassess my above-consensus view if: (1) management signals a pause or slowdown in the buyback program due to Couche-Tard acquisition negotiations, (2) North American same-store sales data shows material deceleration from recent peer results (Walmart, Costco), or (3) Q4 guidance suggests gross margin reverts below 24%. The recent news flow provides no material information - all articles are privacy policy notices with no earnings-relevant content. My conviction remains medium-high given the strong quantitative support for the share count thesis, balanced by margin uncertainty.

forecasts.thesis:
My differentiated view versus the Street's $0.19 EPS consensus is anchored in a currency translation disconnect. The consensus appears to embed an unrealistic JPY weakness, masking stronger local currency performance. I project JPY revenue of ¥2.59T (+3.3% QoQ), moderately above the implied consensus of ¥2.433T, driven by historical Q4 seasonality and resilient defensive retail demand evidenced by peers like Costco. However, I've refined my margin outlook downward from my prior forecast. A detailed line-item projection, informed by historical Q4 margin compression patterns, points to an operating margin of ~4.22%. This yields a net income of ~¥68.3B, translating to JPY EPS of ~¥33.0. Using a JPY/USD exchange rate assumption of ~172 (approximating recent spot), this results in a USD ADR EPS of ~$0.19—which coincidentally matches the Street consensus. The critical insight is that the Street's USD number likely embeds a different forex assumption and possibly lower underlying JPY earnings, whereas my model suggests stronger underlying JPY results offset by forex translation. If JPY strengthens versus my assumption, the USD ADR EPS could surprise positively.

My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $0.51 remains 7.3% below Wall Street consensus of $0.55, anchored in the mechanical reality of tax rate normalization that I believe analysts are systematically underweighting. With management's full-year 2026 ETR guidance of 21%, Q1 tax expense should approximate $977M on my estimated $4.65B pretax income - representing ~$870M in incremental tax expense versus Q4's artificially low base. Mobility service revenue should grow low-single-digits supported by postpaid ARPU expansion, while equipment revenue faces typical Q1 seasonal decline of ~35% from the holiday peak. Fiber continues its steady ~250K quarterly net add pace, and business wireline faces structural decline partially offset by enterprise fiber gains. Today's news flow shows mixed institutional positioning with some funds adding (Professional Advisory +36%, Viking +16.5%) while others trim significantly (Gradient -95%), suggesting no clear directional conviction from sophisticated money.

What would change my view: If Q1's effective tax rate comes in materially below 21% (similar to Q1 2025's 22% or lower), my bear case would be invalidated and EPS could approach Street estimates. Additionally, if equipment revenue shows unusual strength or if fiber net adds accelerate meaningfully above 300K, there's upside to my revenue estimate. The strike authorization risk bears monitoring but I'm not modeling operational disruption at this point given no escalation in today's news.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q3 FY2026 forecast of -$0.05 diluted EPS on $385M revenue represents a modest upward revision from my prior $382M revenue estimate, driven by growing confidence in BrewDog US's full-quarter revenue contribution (~$28M) following the confirmed 3/17-18 acquisition close. The key insight driving my variant view is that the Street's -$0.22 consensus is fundamentally broken - it's anchored to historical periods that included massive non-cash goodwill impairments ($1.75B in Q4 2025, $1.14B in Q3 2025) rather than reflecting normalized operations. Tilray has now achieved near-breakeven for two consecutive quarters on an operating basis, and the beverage transformation is bearing fruit.

The critical data points supporting my view: (1) Beverage will represent ~58% of revenue at $225M, up from roughly 50% in FY2025, driven by the completed BrewDog global consolidation across four regions; (2) Management's $1.2B annual revenue guidance (per 3/9 Motley Fool) validates my $380-390M quarterly run rate; (3) The Carlsberg partnership announced 3/3 provides additional distribution leverage in the US market. The stock's recovery from sub-$1 to ~$6.50 improves ATM issuance economics, reducing dilution per dollar raised.

What would change my mind: If BrewDog brand rehabilitation costs prove significantly higher than anticipated (CEO Simon's comments about 'overcoming stigma' are concerning), or if integration challenges manifest in the quarter. The biggest wildcard is whether non-recurring charges related to the acquisition could distort GAAP results - I'm modeling $10M in other expenses for integration but this could vary. My medium conviction reflects execution uncertainty in the simultaneous four-region consolidation, though the underlying business trajectory is clearly improving.

The Street remains anchored to a simplistic historical average, ignoring deteriorating fundamental trends: (1) Inventory overhang ($395.6M in Q2) will constrain revenue growth, projecting a -2.0% QoQ decline to $298M versus consensus of no growth; (2) Gross margin pressure persists (projected 24.4% vs. 26.4% in Q2) due to promotional activity and mix shift; (3) SG&A remains elevated (~$100M) due to ongoing BrewDog integration and brand management costs, limiting operating leverage; (4) Cash burn continues, necessitating further dilutive equity issuance, with share count projected to rise to 115M. However, my view has moderated from my previous forecast because detailed analysis of Q2 cash flow shows the recent $70M equity issuance likely covers near-term burn, reducing the urgency for an even larger raise this quarter, and the seasonal Q3 uptick (holiday pre-stocking) provides a mild revenue cushion. The key data points driving my variant view are the persistent inventory buildup (bearish), the consistent decline in gross margins (bearish), and the ongoing cash burn masked by equity issuance (bearish). I would change my mind if Q3 shows a sharp inventory drawdown, a significant improvement in operating cash flow, or a stabilization of gross margins above 27%.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q2 2026 EPS estimate of $0.01 remains 50% below Wall Street's $0.02 consensus, maintaining my differentiated view on Tanzania's structural mining tax burden and the unpredictability of non-operating items. The Street's consensus implies a normalized 30-35% effective tax rate, which is demonstrably unrealistic given Q1 2026's 111% effective rate. Tanzania's mining tax regime includes a 6% gross revenue royalty (not profit-based), export withholding taxes, and various other levies that create a structural floor on tax costs regardless of reported profitability. Management's continued silence on tax optimization - now 35+ days post-February roadshow with no clarity despite AGM proceedings, Form 6-K filings, and multiple investor communications - suggests no positive developments to announce.

The key Q2 dynamics create offsetting forces: production volume is expected to reach record levels as Buckreef's ramp continues, but this is substantially offset by gold price normalization from Q1's exceptional $3,860/oz realized price to current spot levels around $2,850/oz (-26%). Additionally, the 20M share warrant exercise (while transformative for liquidity at ~$32M cash) creates 6-7% EPS dilution. My model projects $38M revenue (vs. consensus ~$0B likely reflects stale data), strong operating income of $17.1M, but after a conservatively estimated 70% effective tax rate and ~$6M non-operating drag, net income lands at approximately $3.3M or $0.01 EPS.

What would change my view: (1) Management providing concrete guidance showing a path to normalized 30-40% effective tax rates with specific mechanisms, (2) Gold prices recovering above $3,200/oz which would boost both revenue and margins, or (3) Evidence that Q1's 111% effective rate was truly a one-time anomaly rather than structural. Until such evidence emerges, I maintain my below-consensus stance. The stock's recent volatility (21% decline over past week) suggests the market is beginning to recognize these structural challenges, but consensus estimates haven't fully adjusted.

My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $0.24 matches Street consensus, which represents a meaningful revision down from my prior $0.25 estimate. The critical insight driving this adjustment is the continued absence of delivery data as of March 25 - now well beyond the typical disclosure window for strong quarters. Tesla has historically released delivery data within the first few days of April for normal quarters; the delay pattern is consistent with Q1 2025's disaster quarter when deliveries disappointed significantly. I now model ~340K deliveries (down from 350K), which combined with continued pricing pressure and elevated OpEx for FSD development, results in substantially weaker automotive contribution than previously assumed.

The key offset preventing a more bearish forecast remains the Energy segment, which I project at ~$2.6B revenue with 21%+ gross margins. This high-margin business provides critical earnings support as automotive struggles - contributing roughly $550M in gross profit, or approximately 16% of total gross profit despite being only 12% of revenue. The Stellantis Supercharger partnership announcement validates continued Services growth, and I model Services/Other at $2.9B. However, even this margin-accretive business mix shift cannot fully compensate for the automotive headwinds evident in the delayed delivery data.

What could prove me wrong: If delivery data releases in the next few days showing volumes above 360K, that would suggest my bearish volume assumptions are too conservative. Conversely, if the NHTSA probe escalates or China market data shows accelerating share loss to BYD, downside risk to my $0.24 estimate is material. The reduced 92.3% short interest in TSLS inverse ETF suggests bears are covering - potentially a contrarian signal that the worst automotive news is already priced in.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $0.72 remains 1.4% above the Wall Street consensus of $0.71, unchanged from my previous forecast as no material new information has emerged since March 24th. The key differentiating factor in my above-consensus view is operating expense normalization. Q4 2025's operating expenses of $168.7M were clearly elevated due to one-time and seasonal factors: marketing expenses spiked to $6.3M (vs. the typical $2-3M run rate), and year-end accruals inflated other expense categories to $65.1M vs. the $45-47M range seen in Q2-Q3 2025. I project Q1 operating expenses of ~$156M, representing ~$12M in savings that flows directly to pretax income.

The NIM expansion story remains intact and supports revenue growth. Management guided to continued margin expansion on the Q4 call, and I project NIM of 3.55% in Q1 (up 5bps from Q4's 3.50%) driven by continued deposit cost discipline. This translates to net interest income of ~$242M, up from $237.9M in Q4. Combined with stable fee income and the expense normalization, this produces net income of ~$88M and EPS of $0.72 on 121.7M diluted shares. Credit quality remains pristine with no new concerning signals, and the $0.25 quarterly dividend has been confirmed.

My conviction is medium-high but I'm watching several factors that could change my view: (1) any signs of accelerated credit deterioration in CRE would require provision increases, (2) if the Fed signals more aggressive rate cuts, NIM expansion could stall, and (3) if management indicates expense pressures are structural rather than seasonal, my expense normalization thesis would need revision. The recent news about credit and rate worries pressuring regional bank valuations is primarily sentiment-driven rather than fundamentally concerning for UCB specifically.

With UniFirst stock appreciating 50%+ from pre-announcement levels to trade near the acquisition price, virtually all outstanding stock options, RSUs, and performance share awards are now deeply in-the-money. Using treasury stock method accounting required under GAAP, this dramatically increases the diluted share count from the historical ~18M to my estimate of 26.3M shares. Operationally, I expect solid Q2 performance with revenue of $630M (+4.6% YoY) driven by ~3.5% organic growth plus $15M from recent tuck-in acquisitions. Gross margin will compress modestly to 36.0% from 36.7% due to seasonal labor costs, and SG&A will include $3-4M of M&A advisory fees related to the Cintas transaction documentation process.

The key risk to my thesis is that my share count methodology is incorrect - if consensus is right and diluted shares remain near 18.5M, EPS could reach $1.70+, well above my estimate. I would revisit this if the company provides specific guidance on share count treatment or if I find evidence that the equity award dilution is being handled differently than standard treasury stock method would suggest. forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $1.58 maintains a 15.3% premium to the stale Wall Street consensus of $1.37, reflecting Unity Bancorp's systematic pattern of analyst underestimation that the Street has persistently failed to correct. Over the trailing four quarters, UNTY has beaten consensus by an average of +14.4% (Q4 2025: +11.8%, Q3 2025: +9.3%, Q2 2025: +36.4%, Q1 2025: flat), demonstrating that analysts continue to apply generic community bank multiples to a company delivering best-in-class NIM of 4.5% and ROCE of nearly 20%. The recent valuation upgrade to 'very attractive' confirms the market is beginning to recognize what the fundamental data has shown for quarters.

The key driver of my variant view is Unity's superior net interest margin sustainability. While regional bank peers are seeing NIM compression from deposit competition, UNTY's 10-K filing confirmed stable spread income and disciplined deposit pricing. With earning assets now approaching $3.0B and continued loan growth of 10-12% YoY, I project net interest income of $31.5M for Q1, up from $27.3M in Q1 2025. Operating expenses remain well-controlled around $15.8M, and the effective tax rate should normalize to ~21.5% after some quarterly variability.

I would revise my estimate downward if: (1) Q1 shows NIM compression below 4.3%, suggesting deposit competition is worse than indicated; (2) provision expense spikes meaningfully above $2M, indicating credit deterioration; or (3) management guides conservatively on the call, suggesting headwinds they see but haven't disclosed. However, with earnings on April 10 and no material negative developments since my last update, I maintain high conviction in the $1.58 estimate.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $1.11 is $0.01 below Street consensus of $1.12, representing a modestly bearish variant view driven by two key factors the market is underweighting. First, diesel prices have persisted above $5/gallon through March due to the Iran/Strait of Hormuz conflict, creating $100-125M in fuel cost headwinds with only 60-65% recovery through surcharges. This translates to approximately $40-50M of unrecovered fuel costs flowing directly to operating expenses. Second, FedEx's just-announced SameDay Local service represents incremental competitive pressure in the premium delivery segment that may compress yields faster than expected.

The structural transformation story remains intact - Q4 2025's 11.1% operating margin validated Fit to Serve execution, and the Coyote divestiture at $1.025B strengthens the portfolio focus on higher-margin Healthcare logistics. However, these benefits are being masked by geopolitical-driven fuel costs that are likely transitory. My revenue estimate of $21.15B reflects the Coyote removal (~$150M) plus flat-to-modest growth in core package operations. The YoY EPS decline of ~21% (from $1.40 in Q1 2025) reflects both the challenging comp and current headwinds.

Key swing factors that could prove me wrong: if diesel drops below $4.75/gallon in the next 30 days, the fuel headwind shrinks by ~$25-30M which would add ~$0.02-0.03 to EPS. Conversely, if the Iran situation deteriorates further pushing diesel toward $5.50, my estimate could prove too high. I'm maintaining medium conviction given the binary nature of the fuel cost variable.

My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $2.15 represents an 8% DISCOUNT to Street consensus of $2.33, reflecting the material but now LIMITED impact of the Port Arthur refinery explosion. The critical update since my previous forecast ($1.85) is the March 25 news that Valero is preparing to restart the 380,000 bpd facility THIS WEEK - implying only 5-7 days of downtime versus my prior assumption of 3+ weeks. This dramatically reduces the throughput loss from ~25-30M barrels to approximately 2.5-3M barrels, recovering roughly $1.5B in revenue and $0.30 in EPS versus my prior estimate.

However, I remain below consensus because the Street appears to be treating this as a non-event. The reality is that (1) the diesel hydrotreater unit at the epicenter is a high-margin distillate producer that may take longer to fully restore even if crude units restart, (2) emergency response costs of $30-50M will hit Q1 results with insurance recovery likely in Q2+, (3) inventory build during the shutdown creates working capital drag, and (4) management will likely slow buybacks for cash preservation. Additionally, Q1 is seasonally the weakest quarter for refining due to turnaround season and lower driving demand - note that Q1 2025 reported a LOSS of $1.90 per share.

My conviction is MEDIUM - the key swing factor is the actual timeline and completeness of the Port Arthur restart. If all units including the diesel hydrotreater achieve full rates by month-end, upside to $2.30-2.40 exists. Conversely, if hidden damage emerges requiring extended repairs, downside to $1.80-1.90 remains possible. I would revise higher if management confirms full restart with no complications in the next 48 hours.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $1.19 sits 3.3% below Wall Street consensus of $1.23, reflecting continued skepticism about Frontier integration execution in its first full quarter combined with lingering January network outage impacts. While I've revised my estimate up by $0.01 from yesterday's $1.18 based on Goldman Sachs' bullish price target increase to $55 and continued institutional accumulation (Pensionfund Sabic's new $2.16M position), I maintain conviction that Street models are too optimistic on Frontier's revenue contribution. KeyBanc's characterization of Verizon's reporting changes as 'investor-unfriendly' suggests integration visibility challenges that consensus hasn't adequately discounted. CEO Schulman's explicit acknowledgment that the January outage 'did not meet the standard of excellence' signals material customer impact that could manifest in 12-15bps incremental churn.

The Street appears to be modeling Frontier contribution at $2.1B+ for Q1, but I'm at $1.95B given typical integration friction in the first full quarter post-close. This differential alone accounts for ~$0.02-0.03 of my EPS variance vs consensus. Additionally, business segment weakness continues per analyst coverage, and I'm modeling -2% YoY decline which the market may be underweighting given focus on consumer wireless narratives. The elevated interest expense from the $158.5B debt load post-Frontier creates a meaningful earnings headwind that compounds any revenue shortfall.

What would change my view: If Frontier integration metrics disclosed in the upcoming earnings show revenue run-rate above $2.0B quarterly with stable customer retention, I would revise higher toward consensus. Similarly, if January outage churn data comes in below 10bps with minimal customer loss, the wireless segment would outperform my model. The Goldman upgrade and institutional flows suggest some sophisticated investors see upside I may be missing, but I maintain medium conviction in my variant view given the concrete execution concerns validated by recent analyst commentary.

forecasts.thesis:
My Q1 2026 EPS estimate of $1.67 sits marginally above the $1.66 Wall Street consensus, reflecting a balanced view that incorporates both the operational recovery from Q4's weather-driven miss and the significant headwind from tax rate normalization. The key differentiation in my view centers on three factors: (1) Guyana's operational excellence with automated drilling technology is driving structural cost improvements that consensus hasn't fully captured - this represents genuine margin expansion rather than cyclical benefit; (2) the LNG market tightening from Middle East supply disruptions (highlighted in Morgan Stanley's recent upgrade of US LNG exporters) provides incremental gas price support that offsets some crude oil volatility; and (3) Pioneer integration synergies continue tracking ahead of schedule, adding ~$150M quarterly contribution.

However, I'm revising down from my prior $1.68 estimate due to increased oil price volatility creating forecast uncertainty. The Iran conflict situation cuts both ways - BlackRock's Larry Fink warning of 'stark global recession' if oil hits $150/bbl highlights the demand destruction risk that caps upside, while the news of potential conflict resolution is already pressuring Chevron and Exxon shares premarket. Brent realizations averaging $78/bbl (vs my prior $80-82 assumption) remain the primary headwind. The tax rate normalization from Q4's anomalously low 17.7% to a more typical 28-29% represents roughly $0.25 EPS headwind that the market may be underweighting given Q4's favorable tax outcome.

What would change my view: If oil prices break sustainably above $85/bbl without triggering demand concerns, I'd revise up to $1.75+. Conversely, if the Iran situation resolves quickly and Brent drops to $70/bbl, EPS could fall to $1.50-1.55 range. The chemical segment remains the wildcard - any signs of Asian oversupply abating would provide additional upside. The continued institutional accumulation (World Investment Advisors +24.8%, Nordea +9.2%, MassMutual +20.5%) provides supportive flow dynamics but doesn't change fundamentals.

forecasts.thesis:
I maintain my ¥43.50 Q4 2026 EPS estimate, representing a 6.2% discount to Wall Street consensus of ¥46.39. My variant view centers on the pace of operating margin recovery being structurally slower than what consensus implies. While Q4 should see meaningful seasonal improvement from Q3's severely depressed 7.3% operating margin—driven by China weakness and inventory overhang at ¥216.5B—I project only 10.62% recovery versus the 11.2%+ embedded in consensus estimates. The key constraint remains China exposure (~30% of sales) where servo motor pricing is under pressure and demand visibility remains poor.

The revenue trajectory to ¥148.5T reflects normal Q4 seasonality (historically the strongest quarter) with modest Motion Control and Robotics growth offsetting continued China softness. Critically, the ¥216.5B inventory level represents a material overhang that management must work through, limiting gross margin expansion potential. Recent peer commentary from Kadant and Hyster-Yale confirms stable but not accelerating industrial demand in developed markets, while providing no evidence of China recovery. The elevated capex in Q3 (¥19.2B) suggests continued investment in capacity that may not see utilization benefits this quarter.

What would change my view: (1) Evidence of China demand recovery in servo motors/robotics orders, (2) Inventory reduction faster than my ¥6.5B assumption suggesting better demand, or (3) Management guidance upgrade at earnings. Absent these, the Street appears overly optimistic on margin recovery pace. My conviction is medium given the high variability in quarterly results and limited fresh data since my last forecast.

forecasts.thesis:
My variant view remains that the cached consensus revenue ($0.88B) is structurally incompatible with the company’s historical quarterly statements provided here (revenue consistently ~ $125B–$144B except for an anomalous Q2 2026), so forecasting accuracy should come from internal seasonality and margin patterns rather than anchoring to consensus scale. On that internally consistent scale, I forecast Q4 2026 revenue of $140.6B: a seasonal rebound from Q3 2026’s $134.79B, but still modestly below Q4 2025’s $143.99B, reflecting a not-yet-reaccelerating automation cycle in the absence of new filings/guidance in the dataset.

On profitability, I model a partial recovery in gross margin with largely flat SG&A, driving operating income to $12.65B (vs $9.85B in Q3) and net income to $9.85B, or $38.0 EPS on ~259.7M diluted shares. The key swing factor is non-operating/FX: I keep total other income/expense modestly negative (-$0.45B), but this line has been volatile historically and can move EPS materially.

I would change my view if new company-specific guidance/filings show either (a) a clear robotics order inflection (up or down) or (b) confirmation that the absolute revenue scale in this dataset is mis-keyed (e.g., yen vs dollars vs millions), which would require a full re-scaling of the model and invalidate the current level-based forecast.
